metaDescription: Five higher-budget tablet stands compared, from a wide-base gooseneck floor stand to a 72 inch tripod and compact desk folders, with bed, music and desk picks.
introParagraphs: With a roomier budget ceiling, tablet stands stop being small desktop gadgets and start being proper pieces of furniture. This group covers the LanPavilion floor stand with a 15.7 inch gooseneck and a 1.8 kg base, the SAMHOUSING overhead stand with a listed 6 lb base, the XXZU aluminum tripod that rises from 33.07 to 72 inches, the LISEN gravity-hold folder at 15.2 oz, and the Tonmom folding metal stand.

The key divide is floor stands against desk stands. Floor stands reach over a bed or chair and free your hands entirely, but they demand floor space and a heavy base to counter the lever effect of the arm. Desk stands like the LISEN and Tonmom are smaller and fold away, giving up reach in exchange for a tidy footprint and easy storage.

We evaluated every pick based on product specs and buyer feedback, concentrating on base weight, reach, height range and how simple each stand is to adjust for active adults. We also noted where an extra budget does not buy more, since a larger stand is only better if the room and the tablet need it.

products.name: LanPavilion Gooseneck Tablet Floor Stand
products.description:
The LanPavilion is a floor stand built around a wide, heavy base and a gooseneck arm you can bend by hand. The base weighs 1.8 kg and is described as wide, which counters the leverage of the arm and helps it stay upright. The 15.7 inch gooseneck lets you position a tablet over a bed or beside a chair without any tools.

It accepts devices from 4.7 to 13 inches, so it covers phones, standard tablets and a full-size iPad, and the holder is made of metal. The tradeoff is the length of the arm, which at 15.7 inches is shorter than some overhead floor stands and may not reach comfortably over a deep recliner. A gooseneck is also flexible by nature, so a heavy tablet in a thick case can sag a little.

Setup is quick, and the stand is easy to move because it simply sits on the floor. Compared with the SAMHOUSING, which lists a 6 lb base, the LanPavilion's 1.8 kg base is lighter at about 4 lb, but the wide footprint helps compensate. It is the most straightforward stand in this comparison for bedside use, and it takes less room than the XXZU tripod.
products.bestFor: Bedside or armchair use with a flexible arm and a wide base
pros: 15.7 inch arm bends into position by hand
cons: Arm may be short for a deep recliner
Gooseneck can sag with a heavy case

products.name: SAMHOUSING Overhead Tablet Floor Stand
products.description:
The SAMHOUSING arm is designed to reach over a bed, holding a tablet above you so your hands stay free. Height and angle are both adjustable, and the arm stretches to help you place the screen where you want it. The listed 6 lb base is what keeps the arm balanced as it extends.

The overhead position is what makes it appealing for lying down, since it saves your neck from tilting toward a screen in your lap. The tradeoff is that the stand is a larger object than a desk stand and takes up floor space beside the bed. A heavier case or a large tablet at full reach will test the base more than a light one.

Assembly involves attaching the arm and tightening the joints, and the stand is best positioned with the base against the bed frame. Against the LanPavilion, the SAMHOUSING has a heavier base and a longer reach but fewer published specs about screen size. It suits a bed-focused buyer better than the desk-focused LISEN or Tonmom.
products.bestFor: Lying in bed and watching or reading with the tablet overhead
pros: Listed 6 lb base anchors the reach
cons: Takes floor space beside the bed
Large tablets test the base at full reach
Fewer published specs than the LanPavilion

products.name: XXZU 72 Inch Tablet Floor Tripod
products.description:
The XXZU is a floor tripod that doubles as a sheet music stand, and it is the tallest option in this group. It extends from 33.07 to 72 inches using flip locks, so it works for a seated reader or a person standing at a counter. A 360 degree ball head lets you aim the tablet in portrait, landscape or at an angle.

The angle lock has three levels, and at 83 degrees the legs are set for a more stable stance. That makes it useful for music, recipes at the stove, cooking videos and exercise routines where the tablet needs to be at head height. The tradeoff is that a tripod has a larger footprint than a gooseneck, and it is not meant for lying in bed.

Setup involves spreading the legs and setting the flip locks, which is quick once you know the routine. Compared with the LanPavilion, which sits low beside a bed, the XXZU is the better choice for standing or seated use at a height. It also stores flatter than the SAMHOUSING, though its legs still take space in a closet.
products.bestFor: Music stands, kitchen recipes and standing or seated use at head height
pros: 360 degree ball head aims in any direction
Three-level angle lock for a stable stance
Aluminum build works as a music stand
cons: Not designed for use while lying in bed
Flip locks take practice to set smoothly

products.name: LISEN Foldable Tablet Stand
products.description:
The LISEN is a compact desk stand that holds a tablet by gravity, not by clips or magnets. It weighs 15.2 oz, or 0.95 lb, which gives it more mass than a plastic dock, and a bridge screw rod braces the extension so it stays stable when raised. Height and angle both adjust, and the stand folds flat.

Its gravity system relies on the tablet's back tilt, so it needs a firm surface and the right angle or the tablet can slide forward. It is not designed for steep, near-vertical use. The tradeoff is that it is much smaller than the floor stands here, so it cannot reach a bed.

There are no tools to use, though the bridge screw takes a moment to set. Against the Tonmom, the LISEN is simpler and relies on weight rather than a metal base to stay planted. It is a good fit for someone who wants a tidy stand at a desk or table and does not need floor reach.
products.bestFor: A tidy desk or table stand that folds flat after use
pros: Gravity hold needs no clips or magnets
Bridge screw rod braces the extension
cons: Needs correct back tilt on a firm surface
No reach for beds or recliners

products.name: Tonmom Foldable Tablet Stand
products.description:
The Tonmom is a folding desk stand with two rotating shafts and a heavy-duty metal base. The shafts let you set height and angle independently, and the metal base is intended to keep the tablet from shaking or tipping. It folds fully flat, so it moves easily between a desk and a bag.

The two-shaft design provides more positions than a single hinge, which is useful for switching between typing and watching. The tradeoff is that the listing does not state a screen size range or weight, so it is best suited to ordinary tablets. Each joint is also a potential point of loosening over time.

There is nothing to assemble, and it stores in a drawer. Compared with the LISEN, the Tonmom uses a metal base for steadier placement but is less specific about its limits. It is the lowest-cost pick in this group, which makes it the practical choice if you only need a desk stand.
products.bestFor: A simple, lower-cost desk stand that folds flat
pros: Two rotating shafts set height and angle
Metal base adds stability on a desk
cons: Screen range and weight not published
Joints may loosen with heavy use
No reach for bed or floor use

buyingCriteria.explanation: An arm that reaches out is a lever, so the base must be heavy enough to stay upright. Research on floor stands puts roughly 4.5 lb as a minimum for a full-size iPad at full extension, and listed bases run about 5 to 6.6 lb. The SAMHOUSING lists 6 lb, while the LanPavilion lists a 1.8 kg wide base, which is about 4 lb. A shorter arm needs less base, so match the reach you need to the weight available.

Check the supported size range with your case on. The LanPavilion lists 4.7 to 13 inches, which covers a full-size iPad, and many stands top out near 11 inches. Cases add weight and thickness, and manufacturers note that heavier devices may need a heavier base. A stand with room to spare is safer for a large cased tablet.

The XXZU extends from 33.07 to 72 inches, which is the widest range here, and it suits standing and seated use. Gooseneck stands like the LanPavilion offer a more limited height but reach closer to the body. Raising a screen toward eye level is gentler on the neck than holding it low. Choose the range that fits whether you sit, stand or lie down.

Multi-joint arms need to lock without drooping, and ideally adjust one-handed. The XXZU uses flip locks and a three-level angle lock, the Tonmom uses two rotating shafts, and the LISEN uses a bridge screw rod. Arm load limits are rarely published, so a stand that holds your tablet at an angle for several minutes is a good sign. A joint that drifts is the most common long-term complaint.

Arm stands reach farther but need the base pressed against the bed frame. The SAMHOUSING and LanPavilion are floor stands built for bedside use, whereas the LISEN and Tonmom are desk stands. For bed use, measure how far the arm must reach from the base. A desk stand cannot do a floor stand's job, and the reverse is also true.

Floor stands and tripods take space, and a tripod like the XXZU needs room for its legs. Folding stands such as the LISEN at 15.2 oz and the Tonmom store flat in a drawer. If space is tight, a folding stand is easier to live with. If the tablet is in daily use at one spot, a larger stand is fine.

howWeEvaluated.title: Stability and base design
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared base weights and shapes, including the 6 lb SAMHOUSING base, the 1.8 kg LanPavilion base and the LISEN at 15.2 oz. We looked at whether each stand has a way to brace the arm, such as a bridge screw or a three-level lock. Wide, heavy bases scored higher.

howWeEvaluated.title: Reach and height range
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared how far each stand can place a tablet, from the XXZU at 33.07 to 72 inches to the 15.7 inch LanPavilion gooseneck. We also considered whether the reach suits a bed, a chair or a desk. Stands with a clear fit for their intended use scored well.

howWeEvaluated.title: Device compatibility
howWeEvaluated.description: We reviewed the stated screen sizes, such as the LanPavilion at 4.7 to 13 inches. Where a listing was silent, as with the Tonmom, we noted the gap. Stands that explain their limits clearly scored higher.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ease of adjustment
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared how each stand adjusts, from the LanPavilion gooseneck bending by hand to the XXZU flip locks. We favored stands that need no tools and hold their position. Adjustments that are hard to repeat scored lower.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value for the budget
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared what each stand adds against its position in the budget order. The strongest overall pick, the LanPavilion, adds a heavy base and a flexible arm, while the most basic, the Tonmom, adds a simple folding desk stand. We favored stands where the extra spend bought a clear benefit.

cards.label: Floor stands
cards.text: The LanPavilion, SAMHOUSING and XXZU reach beds and chairs, or extend to head height. They need floor space and a heavy base.

cards.label: Desk stands
cards.text: The LISEN and Tonmom fold flat and store easily but cannot reach a bed. They suit a table or desk.

cards.label: Recommendation
cards.text: Pick the LanPavilion if you want a bedside stand and the LISEN if you want a tidy desk.

rows: Tablet that folds away after use

howToChoose.subheading: For Music and Kitchen Use Specifically

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A height range that reaches head level and a ball head that aims the screen. A stable three-point stance matters more than portability.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The XXZU 72 Inch Tripod fits best, with its 33.07 to 72 inch range and 360 degree ball head.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You want a floor stand with a wide base and a flexible arm. The LanPavilion and SAMHOUSING cost more than the Tonmom because they add weight and reach.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You only need a desk stand. The Tonmom and LISEN fold flat and handle most tablets.

faq.q: Which is better for bed use, the LanPavilion or the SAMHOUSING?
faq.a: Both reach over a bed. The SAMHOUSING lists a 6 lb base and an overhead arm, while the LanPavilion has a 1.8 kg wide base and a 15.7 inch gooseneck. The SAMHOUSING suits lying flat, and the LanPavilion suits sitting up in bed.

faq.q: Is a tripod a good idea for a tablet?
faq.a: It is useful if you want the tablet at head height. The XXZU extends from 33.07 to 72 inches and has a ball head. It is not suited to lying in bed, and its legs take floor space.

faq.q: Do I need a heavier base for a large tablet?
faq.a: Yes, a larger tablet and a thick case add weight at the end of the arm. Research suggests roughly 4.5 lb as a minimum for a full-size iPad at full extension. The SAMHOUSING lists 6 lb, which is a safer margin.

faq.q: Can I use these stands for sheet music?
faq.a: The XXZU is described as a sheet music stand and is the best fit. Its height range and angle lock suit seated or standing play. The desk stands are lower and better for reading.

faq.q: How do I keep a gooseneck from sagging?
faq.a: Keep the arm as short as the task allows and avoid extending it with a heavy case. The LanPavilion has a wide base to help. If it still sags, a rigid stand like the Tonmom or LISEN is a steadier option.

faq.q: Is it worth paying more for a floor stand?
faq.a: It is if you use a tablet in bed or from a chair regularly. Floor stands add reach and a heavy base, which desk stands cannot. If you use a tablet mainly on a table, a folding stand is enough.
